events.title: Telegram
events.text:
🔥 Iran lays mines in the Strait of Hormuz targeting the Omani route — reports
Unconfirmed reports indicate at least some of the missiles fired into the Strait of Hormuz tonight carried naval mines — apparently dropped into the corridor through Omani waters that ships have been using to avoid Iranian clearance.
🔶 It is unclear how many mines were launched, or whether the deployment succeeded
🔶 The target appears to be the very route vessels have been using to evade the PGSA's transit requirements
🔶 Iran previously declared a restricted zone extending from the US Navy's blockade line through the strait and into the Persian Gulf
If confirmed, demining the Omani corridor would take time, ships, and sustained commitment from a US Navy that is already stretched to breaking. And every minesweeper sent into that corridor becomes a stationary target for Iranian forces.
Meanwhile, commercial vessels would have no choice but to obey the PGSA's designated safe route — because the alternative now has mines in it. That means Iranian clearance, Iranian paperwork, Iranian terms.

events.text:
🔍🛫 Boeing flags new 737 MAX software glitch affecting landing navigation
Boeing has identified a previously undisclosed software glitch in the 737 MAX that could cause an automated navigation feature to fail during landing, according to the Wall Street Journal, citing company documents.
🌏 The issue emerged from a cockpit software update
🌏 The glitch can occur when flight crews alter their planned flight path after a missed approach
🌏 Southwest and United have asked Boeing not to deliver new 737 MAX aircraft equipped with the affected software
Boeing has been under intense regulatory and safety scrutiny for years — following two fatal 737 MAX crashes in 2018 and 2019 that grounded the fleet worldwide, and a mid-air cabin panel blowout on a nearly new Alaska Airlines MAX 9.
For a manufacturer that has spent years promising a culture change, this is the same story with a new file name: a problem found in documents, disclosed quietly, and answered with questions instead of answers.

🚢 Ships are emailing Iran to apologize for using unauthorized routes through Hormuz
Shipping companies are now formally writing to the Persian Gulf Strait Authority to ask for forgiveness for passing through the Strait of Hormuz without Iran's permission—and blaming the charterers who forced them to do so.
The US claims the strait is open. In reality, shipowners are sending apology emails to Iran, pleading with the PGSA to lift restrictions on their vessels and promising to comply with Iranian regulations in the future.
The PGSA has warned that companies in violation will be added to the Non-Compliance List, which would restrict their vessels' future transit. At least 4 ships have been struck by Iranian missiles and drones in the Strait of Hormuz in the past few hours.
